classification.difficultyReason: Use the scaffolded intersection quadratic to obtain the squared x-coordinate difference, then recognise that the line makes the y-coordinate difference equal to it before applying distance.

content.prompt: The circle $x^2+y^2=16$ and the line $y=x+2$ meet at points $P(x_1,y_1)$ and $Q(x_2,y_2)$.

spec.sourceRegion: Question 64, left column, figure between the stem and part (a).
spec.description: Unshaded circle centred at the origin, intersected by an ascending line. Positive axes have arrowheads; the line has arrowheads at both ends. Black intersection markers and labels P, Q, x and y; no ticks or grid.
spec.mathematics: Circle x^2+y^2=16; line y=x+2. P=(-1-sqrt(7),1-sqrt(7)) and Q=(-1+sqrt(7),1+sqrt(7)) locate the supplied markers without printing their coordinates.
spec.answerVisibility: Only the source-supplied loci, point markers and labels are visible; no numerical intersection coordinates or answers are printed.

children.label: a
children.prompt:
Show that $x_1$ and $x_2$ must satisfy the equation
$$x^2+2x-6=0.$$

answer.short: Substitute $y=x+2$ into $x^2+y^2=16$ and simplify to obtain $x^2+2x-6=0$.
answer.worked:
Substitute $y=x+2$ into the circle equation.
$$\begin{align*}
x^2+(x+2)^2&=16\\
2x^2+4x+4&=16\\
2x^2+4x-12&=0\\
x^2+2x-6&=0
\end{align*}$$
Both intersection points lie on the line and circle, so their $x$-coordinates $x_1$ and $x_2$ satisfy this equation.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Hence, find the exact distance of $PQ$.

answer.short:
$PQ=2\sqrt{14}$.

Since $y=x+2$, the squared coordinate differences are both $28$; apply the distance formula.
answer.worked:
Both points lie on $y=x+2$, so
$$\begin{align*}
y_1-y_2&=(x_1+2)-(x_2+2)\\
y_1-y_2&=x_1-x_2.
\end{align*}$$
Thus $(y_1-y_2)^2=28$. By the distance formula,
$$\begin{align*}
PQ&=\sqrt{(x_1-x_2)^2+(y_1-y_2)^2}\\
PQ&=\sqrt{28+28}\\
PQ&=2\sqrt{14}.
\end{align*}$$
